quote:
An example corroborating the importance of conservation location is from riparian
buffer simulations. Despite an overall positive correlation between the size of the buffer
and the amount of sediment reduction, Figure 11 shows that scenarios 4 and 12 use an
almost equal buffer surface area (i.e., 338 and 357.9 ha, respectively) but lead to a large
difference in sediment load reduction (i.e., 45% and 15%, respectively).

relationship.outcome_raw: Reduction in annual average sediment load at watershed outlet relative to no-buffer model baseline; paired placement comparison

context.region: North Fork Forked Deer River watershed, West Tennessee
context.practice_as_described: Constructed riparian vegetation buffers, 10 m source-reported width, beside all streams adjacent to agricultural fields; compared with model baseline with no buffer integrated. Width side convention unresolved.
context.note: Table 4 (p17), Riparian buffer scenarios results, scenario 4: outlet load 113389.3 Mg/year; footprint 338.0 ha. Baseline 205880.2 Mg/year. Annualized Agricultural Non-Point-Source (AnnAGNPS) model; no observed streamflow or sediment gauges (p16), not measured causal field effect. Mechanism: slowing surface flow promotes infiltration and fine sediment deposition (p18). Inter-rill/rill sources only; channel erosion held constant (p22). All scenarios belong to ONE model study, not independent replicates. Scenario-specific values retained, no pooled percentage. Outcome is watershed-scale sediment export reduction, not direct within-buffer trapping efficiency; VONT sediment_retention alias sediment reduction. Related scenario EV IDs are companion claims, not independent studies. Process: remaining Table 4 rows and contradictory narrative metrics retained in inventory; no full-source completion claimed.

justification_quote:
Riparian buffers work by slowing surface ﬂow and promoting inﬁltration and ﬁne
sediment deposition.
